reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The .369 xwOBA and .497 xSLG at the 93rd percentile each tell the same story: when he makes contact, he does real damage, and the 13.1% barrel rate backs that up. The problem is he chases at 34.1% and strikes out at 26.1%, which is how you end up with an xBA sitting at .259 while the xSLG reads .497 — he's a power hitter whose swing decisions cost him a significant chunk of what his raw quality of contact would otherwise buy. Add 29.5 ft/s sprint speed and an 11.5% walk rate, and the projection's 43 home runs and 37 steals in 721 plate appearances become believable if the contact rate holds at roughly its current shape. The whole profile hinges on whether he can trim the chase rate even modestly; if he can't, the strikeouts will suppress the average enough to flatten the counting stats, but the power and speed floor still leaves a high-upside regular even in the pessimistic version.

reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-four home runs projected at age 23 is a statement, and the Statcast profile backs it: a 93.1 mph average exit velocity ranks in the 96th percentile, and his 50.5% hard-hit rate pairs with a 13.0% barrel rate to sketch a true middle-of-the-order bat. The 11.7% walk rate is legitimately above average, his K% sits at 18.3%, and the xwOBA of .365 reflects contact quality that the raw slash already anticipates. Everything here hinges on his ability to hold pitchers accountable in the zone — the chase and whiff rates are league-average at best, so if opponents find a way to exploit that, the strikeouts climb and the walks evaporate with them. If the discipline holds, though, he's a front-of-the-lineup power threat who makes the Rays look very smart.

reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: The gap between his 13.6% barrel rate and his 38.7% hard-hit rate tells you almost everything: Stewart makes elite contact when he squares it up, but he doesn't square it up as often as that hard-hit number implies. The .484 xSLG sits at the 90th percentile and lines up cleanly with the projection's .486 SLG across a full 702 plate appearances, which is the part of this profile worth trusting. His 27.0% whiff rate and 30.7% chase rate are ordinary enough that the profile doesn't hinge on a plate-discipline correction, it hinges on whether the barrel rate holds as pitchers learn him. If it does, the projected 36 home runs and .822 OPS are a reasonable floor for a 22-year-old first baseman settling into a lineup.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The .402 xwOBA and 2.72 xERA exist in the same body, which still hasn't stopped being remarkable. On the hitting side, the contact profile carries a real tension: a 15.9% barrel rate and 93.4 mph average exit velocity sit in a frame that also posts a 30.9% whiff rate, meaning he punishes mistakes at an elite level but can be put away, and the 13.2% walk rate is what keeps the .379 OBP honest when the bat misses. On the mound, a 98.1 mph fastball paired with 30.4% whiff rate and a contact profile that holds opponents to an 87.4 mph average exit velocity explains the xERA; the 7.6% walk rate is the one lever that could loosen the whole thing if it climbs. The projection of .279/.379/.534 with 37 home runs as a DH while returning to a rotation is only remarkable because we've stopped being surprised by it.

reports.name: Jordan Walker
reports.published_report: The contact metrics and the contact outcomes are pointing in opposite directions, and that's the whole Walker puzzle. His 92.4 mph average exit velocity sits in the 92nd percentile and his barrel rate is 13.5%, but a 35.9% chase rate and 30.8% whiff rate are bleeding the profile — both near the bottom fifth of the league. The power translates regardless: .483 xSLG says the raw damage is there when he makes contact, and a full season of that shape carries to a projected .488 SLG over 668 plate appearances with 31 home runs. Everything hinges on whether pitchers keep exploiting the zone-recognition issues or Walker tightens the chase rate enough to let the exit-velocity profile breathe fully.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The contact metrics and the exit velocity tell two completely different stories, and the exit velocity wins. At 93.9 mph average exit velo with a 14.0% barrel rate and 50.9% hard-hit rate, De La Cruz hits the ball as hard as almost anyone in the league, and the xwOBA of .361 with xSLG of .473 reflect that contact quality far more honestly than the 27.2% strikeout rate that makes casual observers nervous. A 10.9% walk rate keeps the on-base from cratering, and the projection's .349 OBP across 638 plate appearances shows a player who has learned enough zone discipline to let the damage play. Twenty-five projected home runs alongside 29 stolen bases makes for one of the more complete offensive profiles at shortstop, and the whole thing hinges on that strikeout rate not drifting higher: if it does, the .269 average erodes and the .824 OPS follows it down.

reports.name: Jackson Merrill
reports.published_report: The contact quality is legitimate and the speed earns its reputation, but the plate discipline is the ceiling question. Merrill's .466 xSLG and 46.6% hard-hit rate show genuine thump for a 23-year-old outfielder, and his 29.0 ft/s sprint speed puts him in elite company on the bases, which is how the projection gets to 26 home runs and 27 stolen bases across 666 PA. What drags the projection OPS down to .719 is a 37.5% chase rate that turns all that hard contact into a 6.5% walk rate, leaving him perpetually exposed to pitchers willing to work the zone's edge. If he ever learns to lay off, the xSLG is there for something better; if he doesn't, he's a power-speed outfielder with a below-average on-base that caps him as a solid regular and nothing more.

reports.name: Jackson Chourio
reports.published_report: The contact-to-power gap is the whole tension here. At 92.0 mph average exit velocity, 13.1% barrel rate, and 47.9% hard-hit rate, the raw thump is genuine and consistent, and the .467 xSLG backs it up. But a 34.0% chase rate is doing real damage to everything downstream: the xBA sits at .255, the walk rate at 8.2%, and the strikeout rate at 23.9%, which is why a hitter with this kind of exit velo profiles as a .336 xwOBA rather than something scarier. The projection (.278/.339/.474, 24 HR) is a fair translation of that gap — a plus-speed, plus-raw-power player who gets a little less than his bat deserves because pitchers can get him to expand. If the chase rate tightens even modestly as he moves deeper into his age-22 season, this becomes a true middle-of-the-order piece; if it doesn't, he's a very good player with an avoidable ceiling.

reports.name: Eli Willits
reports.published_report: Ninety-one walks at A+ & A as an 18-year-old is the number that rewrites the whole profile. The walk rate sits at 18%, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts that discipline at 12.9%, well clear of the 8.5% MLB average, which means the plate approach isn't a byproduct of soft competition. Fifty-seven stolen bases across A+ & A give the profile a second gear the slash line doesn't fully express, though the ISO translation is where the ceiling question lives: .187 in the minors shrinks to a .128 equivalent, and MLB average ISO runs at .150, so the everyday-regular outcome runs through the hit tool and speed holding as he climbs rather than any power breakout. If the walk rates compress and the legs don't translate, a bench piece built around on-base skills is the honest floor.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.1 ERA and a 0.6 WHIP at Double-A aren't numbers that need context — they're the argument. Anderson has struck out 135 batters against 13 walks across 93.3 innings at AA this season, and the command profile translates cleanly: a BB/9 of 2.0 in MLB terms, well below the 3.2 figure where most pitchers land, with a K-BB% that comes out to 21.9% against an average of 13.5%. The whole thing hinges on whether the stuff backs up the control at the highest level, because a left-hander this young who misses this many bats while almost never missing the zone has no obvious developmental ceiling short of a frontline starter. If the stuff softens in the jump, he's still a useful mid-rotation arm, but nothing in this line suggests you should expect softening.

His xSLG sits at .428 on the current MLB line, a meaningful gap below the .495 SLG ValuCast is projecting across a full season — the bet is that the power translates further than the contact metrics suggest it should. That 36.9% chase rate is the thing: it suppresses the xBA to .246 and keeps the whiff rate at 29.1%, so a .264 AVG with this discipline profile requires either a meaningful chase improvement or a lot of loud contact on the balls he does make. At 28.5 ft/s the speed fits the 30-steal projection cleanly, and if the power holds closer to projection than to current xSLG, you're looking at a genuine 30-30 shortstop posting an .834 OPS; if the chase rate stays where it is, the counting-stat ceiling deflates and you're building around the legs instead.

reports.name: Gunnar Henderson
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is almost aggressively median — xwOBA at .319, barrel rate at 7.2%, walk rate at 9.3%, strikeout rate at 21.5%, all clustering right around the middle of the league. What separates Henderson is contact quality that outpaces his expected outcomes: a 44.2% hard-hit rate in the 71st percentile while his xBA sits at .245, which tells you the damage exists but isn't concentrated in the barrels that drive slugging. The projection's .228 AVG with 26 home runs across 718 plate appearances is the honest shape of that profile, a hitter whose power shows up in runs and HR totals but whose batting average bleeds enough to keep the OPS at .725. He's an everyday shortstop with above-average speed and a solid glove, and the ceiling question is whether the hard contact starts landing in places that lift the xwOBA off the 47th percentile.

reports.name: Michael Harris II
reports.published_report: The .288 xBA sits at the 95th percentile, and the gap between that and his actual average is the whole argument for Harris. He puts the ball hard into play, a 48.5% hard-hit rate, and his contact quality is legitimate, but a 44.8% chase rate and 3.6% walk rate, both near the bottom of the league, mean he's living entirely on his ability to do damage when he swings. If pitchers find a reliable way to exploit that aggression, the .294 projection evaporates; if they can't, you get 27 home runs, an .818 OPS, and a center fielder whose OAA percentile sits at 97. He's already the profile, as long as the bat-to-ball keeps outrunning the zone-discipline problem.

reports.name: Walker Jenkins
reports.published_report: The contact rate is the headline: 15% strikeouts across AAA & A+ & A translates to 18.7% at the MLB level, well below where most big-league hitters land, and that's with a .237 ISO in tow. At 21, Walker Jenkins is posting a .417 OBP across those three levels while walking 43 times against only 50 strikeouts in 324 plate appearances, a combination that scouts get excited about precisely because disciplined hitters with real power don't usually need much fixing. The ISO translates to .171 at the MLB equivalent, above what most regulars produce, so the power isn't a minor-league mirage, but his ceiling as an everyday center fielder depends on how much of that contact quality survives a full diet of big-league velocity. If it doesn't hold, you're looking at a useful bench piece; if it does, the Twins have a true regular.

reports.name: Paul Skenes
reports.published_report: The 3.12 xERA tells the real story here: the projection's 3.67 ERA is the pessimistic read on a pitcher who already suppresses hard contact well below what his strikeout rate would suggest he needs to. A 29.5% strikeout rate at the top of the percentile ladder, paired with a 6.9% walk rate that sits comfortably in the upper quarter — that's a profile where the miss is genuine and the zone is mostly on his terms. The one thing worth watching is barrel rate and hard-hit percentage that land closer to league average than the rest of the card, which means the gap between his xERA and his ERA closes or widens depending on how much the defense and sequencing cooperate across a full projected workload. If contact suppression tightens to match the strikeout dominance, you're looking at a front-of-rotation horse; if the hard-hit numbers drift upward, the projection's 3.67 is the floor, not the ceiling.

reports.name: Cam Schlittler
reports.published_report: The fastball sitting at 98.0 mph with 2532 rpm of spin is doing most of the heavy lifting, and the strikeout rate backs it up: he's punching out batters at a 30.9% clip while walking just 6.5%. The xwOBA of .268 and xERA of 2.96 say the underlying quality is genuine, not a strand-rate mirage, and a 190.4-inning projection at a 2.28 ERA suggests ValuCast sees the workload holding. The one honest wrinkle is that his hard-hit and barrel numbers sit near league average, meaning he lives and dies by missing bats rather than inducing weak contact, so if that 30.9% strikeout rate softens, the profile changes shape in a hurry.

reports.name: Jac Caglianone
reports.published_report: The contact quality here is about as loud as it gets: 93.2 mph average exit velocity and a 54.8% hard-hit rate both sit near the top of the league, and the .513 xSLG translates to genuine middle-of-the-order thump even before the projection's 27 home runs come into view. The whole thing hinges on whether he can cut a 39.0% chase rate that currently grades near the bottom of the league, because a 26.0% strikeout rate paired with a 5.9% walk rate is a thin margin for a guy who needs at-bats to do damage. If the plate discipline tightens even modestly, the raw contact quality makes a .828 OPS look conservative; if it doesn't, he's a middle-of-the-order profile that pitchers keep running off the plate with stuff in the zone.

reports.name: Juan Soto
reports.published_report: A .422 xwOBA and a 20.0% chase rate tell you almost everything — he makes elite contact on the balls he swings at and simply refuses to chase the rest. reports.name: Julio Rodríguez
reports.published_report:
The gap between what Julio Rodríguez does to the ball and what he does with his at-bats is the whole profile. His xSLG sits at .451 and his xBA at .266, both in the upper quarter of the league, yet a 39.1% chase rate drags the actual production back toward ordinary, and the projection settles at .248/.309/.412.

The contact quality is genuine: 90.0 mph average exit velocity, 43.4% hard-hit rate, and a .340 xWOBA all say a true-talent hitter is in there. The speed (28.7 ft/s, 86th percentile) adds another dimension that keeps the floor from being just a slugging-only profile. But the walk rate sits at 7.4% and the chase at 39.1%, which is a pairing that bleeds value every time pitchers stay off the plate, and there's no projection of zone discipline improving in the numbers here.

If the plate approach tightens, the underlying contact metrics support a breakout; if it doesn't, 25 home runs and 20 steals in 654 projected PA is a useful player who never quite became the star the tools implied.

reports.name: Tyler Bremner
reports.published_report: The K-BB% is the number that carries this profile: 24% across AA & A+, which translates to a MLB-equivalent 14.6% when the level adjustment is applied. Bremner has struck out 92 batters in 68.3 innings while walking only 25, and that command-to-stuff ratio lands in the 96th percentile of his pitcher pool. The translated BB/9 sits at 3.6, just above the MLB mark of 3.2, so the control that looks clean in the minors has a little give in it when leveled up. If the walk rate holds anywhere near its current shape, he works as a back-end starter; if it softens, the strikeout rate still plays in a bullpen role.

reports.name: Daylen Lile
reports.published_report: That 38.4% chase rate is the load-bearing wall, and everything else in the Statcast card bends around it. His xBA and xSLG are both well above average when he makes contact, and 29.3 ft/s sprint speed puts him in elite company on the bases, but the walk rate sits at 6.3% while he's chasing nearly four pitches in ten outside the zone. If pitchers keep feeding him breaking balls off the edge and he keeps biting, the .310 OBP in the projection becomes a floor fantasy. Make the swing decisions even slightly more disciplined and the contact quality, xSLG at .445 with K% a reasonable 18.8%, turns him into a legitimate everyday outfielder with 23 home runs and 15 steals in a full season; stay undisciplined and he's a second-division regular kept afloat by his legs and his bat when he connects.

reports.name: Zach Neto
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile has two faces that don't fully reconcile: an 11.8% barrel rate that grades out well, sitting alongside a 33.3% whiff rate and 37.6% chase rate that both bottom out near the league floor. When he makes contact, there's genuine pop, and 27 home runs across 701 plate appearances is a realistic outcome. But the xBA of .208 tells you how rarely that contact comes, and the gap between a .403 xSLG and a .306 xwOBA is the whole tension in the profile, power that keeps getting taxed by empty swings before it can accumulate. If the chase rate stays where it is, the projected .236 average is probably optimistic, and you're left with a shortstop whose value lives almost entirely in the power-and-speed combination, 27 home runs and 22 steals at a position where that shape still plays even at .236.

reports.name: Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
reports.published_report: The contact ability is legitimate and the power isn't keeping up with it. Guerrero's 12.7% strikeout rate sits in rarefied air for a first baseman, and his xBA of .282 reflects genuine bat-to-ball skill, but a 6.5% barrel rate and .397 xSLG tell you the pop that once made him a feared middle-of-the-order presence has quietly flattened out near league average. The projection lands at 11 home runs across 619 plate appearances, which is a damning number for a corner bat with his pedigree. If the barrel rate climbs back toward what his exit velocity and contact quality suggest is possible, you get a solid everyday first baseman; if it doesn't, what's left is a high-average, low-damage regular who is increasingly hard to roster at full value.

reports.name: Chase Burns
reports.published_report: The 31.5% whiff rate and 35.1% chase rate tell you what Burns is: a pitcher who makes hitters swing and miss, not one who avoids hard contact when they do connect. The exit-velocity and hard-hit numbers sit right around league average, so when he leaves something over the plate, it gets hit. reports.name: Cristopher Sánchez
reports.published_report: The chase rate tells you most of what you need to know: 36.8% puts him in the 96th percentile, and the 32.8% whiff rate isn't far behind. Sánchez doesn't overpower hitters, the exit velocity profile is middling, but he gets them to swing at pitches they shouldn't, then miss when they do, and he almost never puts himself in trouble voluntarily at 5.4% walks. The Statcast xERA of 3.24 is the honest floor; if the chase-and-whiff engine holds, a 204.8-inning season with 233 strikeouts and a 2.57 ERA is what the upside looks like. The one thing to watch is hard contact when hitters do make contact, 41.8% hard-hit is the crack in an otherwise clean profile, and the day his command slips enough to let hitters sit on pitches is the day it matters.

reports.name: Royce Lewis

reports.name: JJ Bleday
reports.published_report: The gap between his .348 xwOBA and a .218 projected average tells you almost everything. Bleday's 13.9% walk rate is genuinely elite, his 22.2% chase rate puts him in rarefied company among contact avoiders, and those two things together are what drive that xwOBA north of a hitter who barely bats his weight. The issue is that 88.5 mph average exit velocity — the contact quality when he does swing doesn't match the plate discipline profile, which is why .244 xBA and .329 OBP coexist in the same body. If the power holds at or near 25 home runs in a full season, he's a useful everyday outfielder whose walks paper over a batting average most managers would wince at; if the home run rate softens, what's left is a patient bat that doesn't hit the ball hard enough to carry a lineup spot on its own.

reports.name: Masyn Winn
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile splits cleanly in two: elite plate discipline, no juice. Winn's 24.2% chase rate sits at the better end of the league, his strikeout and walk rates are right at the middle of the pack, and the contact itself is fine — a .248 xBA that lands exactly at the median. But a 3.6% barrel rate and 35.0% hard-hit rate are bottom-quartile power numbers, and the .333 xSLG confirms there's almost nothing to drive. The projection at .240/.315/.333 reflects that split honestly: a shortstop who won't beat himself, plays elite defense by OAA, and runs well at 28.4 ft/s, but whose offensive ceiling is constrained almost entirely by whether the bat-to-ball skills and speed can manufacture value that the raw contact quality won't. If the discipline holds and the legs age gracefully, he's a second-division regular who helps himself on the bases and never kills a lineup; if the power floor doesn't tick up at all as he matures, the profile slides toward a good-glove bench piece who starts against lefties.

reports.name: Trevor Rogers
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the best thing about this profile, and it mostly holds the whole thing together. Rogers gets chases at a 34.5% clip, an 87th-percentile mark, but hitters don't whiff at 23.6% when they do swing, which is why the strikeout rate sits at a below-average 20.9%. He's a contact manager more than a swing-and-miss arm, and with 2475 rpm of fastball spin he can generate weak contact when his command keeps the ball in favorable counts. The xERA of 3.85 says the underlying contact profile is better than a 4.34 projection implies, but that gap closes fast if his 6.4% walk rate creeps up and hitters stop chasing, leaving a back-end starter with average stuff and no strikeout margin to spare.

reports.published_report: The fastball reads like the foundation of a real mid-rotation starter: 96.0 mph with 2398 rpm of spin, both sitting well above the middle of the league. The problem is everything downstream from the pitch itself — a 20.8% strikeout rate and a 22.6% whiff rate that trail the bulk of the rotation-starter population, which means the stuff isn't converting to swing-and-miss the way you'd expect it to. Contact quality suppression is doing some of the damage control, with a 6.4% barrel rate, but a 41.6% hard-hit rate and a 90.2 mph average exit velo keep the floor low enough that a 4.02 xERA is about where he actually lives. reports.name: José Soriano
reports.published_report: The 30.1% whiff rate is loud, but the 10.6% walk rate is the whole argument against him. Soriano generates chase at a solid clip and misses bats at a rate that puts him ahead of most starters, yet he can't locate well enough to convert that stuff into outs efficiently, which is exactly why his xERA sits at 4.46 while the projection asks you to believe in a 3.49. The fastball at 97.1 mph is the foundation, but 2178 rpm spin keeps it from playing as a true weapon, so the whiffs are coming from deception and movement he has to land for strikes, and when he misses, hitters wait. If the walk rate tightens, a mid-rotation starter is plausible across the 178.3 projected innings; if it stays at 10.6%, you're looking at a back-end arm burning deep counts until a lineup turns him over.

reports.name: Bryce Harper
reports.published_report: The .393 xwOBA tells you everything about why the raw numbers look modest: Harper doesn't create value by beating barrels into the ground, he creates it by not giving pitchers anything free. A 16.4% walk rate puts him at the very top of the league, and pitchers who try to dance around him pay for it when he does connect, with an xSLG of .504 backing the projection's .503 SLG almost to the decimal. The contact profile is the one wrinkle — a 29.8% whiff rate against a K% that sits near average means he's making more weak contact than the damage numbers suggest, and the gap between a 74th-percentile exit velocity and a 95th-percentile xSLG is entirely a function of plate discipline pulling the expected outcomes up. If the walk rate erodes with age, what remains is a hitter with real but not elite contact quality; if it holds, the projection's .888 OPS at 692 plate appearances is exactly what a healthy 33-year-old version of this profile produces.

Parker's contact quality is where the ceiling closes in: the ISO translates to .126 in MLB-equivalent terms, meaningfully short of where hitters need to be to profile as regulars, which means the power reading at this level is more about a hitter's count than a legitimate gap threat. The 26 stolen bases add a real dimension, but if the bat-to-ball doesn't sharpen as the pitching gets sharper, you're left with a patient shortstop who can't do enough damage to force his way into an everyday lineup.

reports.name: Gabriel Gonzalez
reports.published_report: The translation is the problem. Gonzalez is hitting .254 with 15 home runs at AAA in 444 plate appearances, and the raw line reads like a useful bat, but the MLB-equivalent ISO comes out to .14, essentially matching what the average MLB hitter produces, and the walk rate drops from 8% at AAA to 7.7% when translated. The strikeout rate actually plays better than it looks: 18% at AAA translates to 20.2%, comfortably under the MLB mean of 22.0%, so the contact profile is his best carry. Everything hinges on whether that below-average power holds its shape against better stuff, because if the ISO erodes further, the bat doesn't have the on-base or speed profile to compensate. Either a fringe bench bat if the contact holds, or pure organizational depth if the power thins out.

reports.name: Sterlin Thompson
reports.published_report: The .470 OBP is the whole argument, and then you look at the walk rate and understand it: 66 walks against 54 strikeouts across 332 AAA plate appearances, a 20% walk rate that translates to 14.6% at the MLB level while the typical big-league hitter walks less than half that often. The contact reads similarly well, a .315 average with 16 stolen bases layered on top, but the MLB-equivalent ISO lands right at league average, and that's where the ceiling caps out. If the strike zone command translates, Thompson is a left-handed bench bat who gets on base at a rate that makes him genuinely useful; if pitchers at the big-league level find his edge, the profile without carrying power shrinks fast to a depth role.

reports.name: Will Warren
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile has one genuinely loud number and one genuinely ugly one, and those two facts tell you almost everything. His fastball spin sits at 2537 rpm, a figure that lands in the 91st percentile, yet the hard-hit rate against him is 44.6%, near the bottom of the league, which means the spin isn't translating into weak contact the way you'd expect. The xERA of 4.49 and xwOBA of .326 both land in the 29th percentile, so the current ERA projection of 4.20 across 159.9 innings is probably a little generous to him. He gets the ball into the zone (7.8% walk rate is slightly better than league average) and misses enough bats to stay in rotations, but a 22.3% whiff rate and 28.7% chase rate suggest the spin plays better on paper than in outcomes, and if the hard-hit profile doesn't improve, he's a back-of-rotation innings-eater on a team that can afford to ask for more.

reports.name: Yandy Díaz
reports.published_report:
A 14.6% whiff rate at age 35 is the Díaz profile in a single number: elite contact against ordinary power, and the formula still produces .826 OPS in the projection.

The Statcast card explains why. A .284 xBA grades out sharply above the league, and a 47.6% hard-hit rate shows the ball gets hit firmly even when the barrel rate sits at a modest 7.0%, meaning his damage comes from volume of hard contact rather than peak loft. The projection at 698 PA reflects exactly that shape, a first baseman who hits for a high average and generates 24 home runs without being a true slugger. Everything hinges on that contact skill aging gracefully; if the whiff rate creeps up, an 8.3% walk rate doesn't compensate, and he slides quickly from solid regular toward a DH posting a line well south of .826.

reports.name: Spencer Torkelson
reports.published_report: The barrel rate is the only place Torkelson's Statcast card looks healthy — except that's an em-dash, so: his 12.3% barrel rate lands in the 81st percentile, and it's doing almost all the carrying. A 31.5% strikeout rate at the 5th percentile drags the xBA down to .212, and no amount of hard contact survives that kind of contact suppression across a full season. His 22.0% chase rate shows he's identifying pitches well enough to run an 11.1% walk rate, which makes the whiff rate on pitches he does offer at the dependency worth watching: if that number comes down, you get a second-division regular with pop; if it stays, 24 home runs in a .717 OPS season is what a rebuilding team pencils in and quietly hopes to replace.

reports.name: Gage Jump
reports.published_report: The fastball grades out well, 96.2 mph and 2363 rpm put him in the upper quarter of starters on both counts, but everything downstream of that pitch is where the profile gets uncomfortable. His 11.1% walk rate is the problem that swallows the rest: the strikeouts are roughly league average at 24.3%, the whiff rate sits exactly at the median, and hitters who do make contact are punishing it, with a .327 xwOBA and 4.52 xERA that both land near the bottom third of the league. If he ever sharpens the command enough to push that walk rate toward something functional, the raw stuff gives him a real starting profile to work with. Until then, the projection reads like what it probably is: a 4.96 ERA across 117.5 innings, a back-end arm held back by his own hand.

reports.name: Jacob Berry
reports.published_report: The contact is the whole case. At AAA this year across 366 plate appearances, Berry has struck out just 15% of the time, which translates to an 18.2% MLB-equivalent clip against a league that whiffs at 22.0% — that's a real edge, and it's paired with 49 walks against only 55 strikeouts, a discipline profile that doesn't often survive the translation intact. The power, though, is the ceiling-capper: a .139 ISO at AAA translates to .125 against big-league arms, well below average, and 8 home runs in 366 PA doesn't hint at a hidden gear waiting to emerge. If the contact and walk rates hold at the big-league level, he's a useful bench bat who gets on base; if the ISO doesn't tick up at all, there's no everyday profile here, just a very patient fourth outfielder.

reports.name: Riley Quick
reports.published_report: 103 strikeouts across AA & A+ & A this season, and the K/9 of 12.8 sits at the 92nd percentile of his pool — the swing-and-miss reads as real across three levels and 72.6 innings. At 19, Chase Harlan is doing real plate discipline work, 51 walks in 396 PA, and the .298/.403/.509 line puts him at the 93rd percentile in OPS among this hitter pool. The translation is where it gets honest: his ISO drops from .211 to .137 MLB-equivalent, below league average, and his strikeout rate lands at 25.4% where the MLB average sits at 22.0, so the power that reads as a weapon at A-ball may arrive as fringe-average at the highest level. reports.name: Noah Cameron

His 26.3% whiff rate is carrying the strikeout work that his velocity can't, but the 21.0% K% still lands below average, and his chase rate of 29.2% suggests hitters aren't extending much trouble outside the zone. What's keeping him functional is the contact quality: a 7.9% barrel rate and 88.8 mph average exit velo land right around league average, plus a 7.7% walk rate that won't kill a start. That ISO deflates to .175 in MLB equivalent terms, and the strikeout rate climbs from 24% in AAA to 25% translated, while the walk rate lands at 8.7%, nearly identical to the MLB mean of 8.5%. There's no on-base cushion to absorb the swing-and-miss, and at 1B, a profile that lives and dies by raw power needs the bat to carry everything. If the power doesn't translate past .175 ISO, what's left is a bench bat or organizational depth, which is exactly where ValuCast sees the ceiling landing.

reports.name: Chad Patrick
reports.published_report: The 3.44 ERA projection looks charitable against a 4.11 xERA from his current Statcast profile. His barrel suppression is the one thing working in his favor, a 6.2% barrel rate that grades well above average, but a 9.8% walk rate undercuts the whole thing, because you can suppress hard contact all day and still hand runs back on free passes. The 20.9% strikeout rate isn't enough to bail him out when he falls behind, and his chase rate sits near league average, so he's not generating the early counts that let pitchers absorb their own walks. A backend reliever with a functional ERA if the walk rate stabilizes; if it doesn't, that 4.11 xERA is closer to what you're actually getting.

reports.name: Braden Davis
reports.published_report: Eleven strikeouts per nine innings at AA is loud enough to make you lean in, but 68 walks across 102.7 innings is the reason you lean right back out. The strikeout rate translates to 9.1 per nine in an MLB context, a tick above league average, but the walk rate translates to 5.5, nearly double what big-league starters absorb as a baseline. The K-BB% at 14% at AA is the honest reconciliation of those two forces, and it says the stuff that misses bats can't yet find the zone reliably enough to matter. Command consolidation is the one dependency: if it comes, he becomes a depth arm with a real out-pitch; if it doesn't, the 130 strikeouts are a footnote on a 5.1 ERA that never moved.

reports.name: Vinnie Pasquantino
reports.published_report: The contact profile is genuinely elite — a 15.6% whiff rate and 16.0% strikeout rate that put him among the better bat-to-ball first basemen in the league, but the power just isn't there to carry a corner. His xSLG sits at .412, which is fine, not fearsome, and the projection's 12 home runs across 480 PA tells you the gap between contact quality and actual damage is the whole tension in this profile. If the exit velocity (89.6 mph, right at league average) ever ticks up and the barrel rate grows beyond 7.6%, he becomes a .335 OBP, above-average regular worth building around; if it doesn't, he's a disciplined, bat-first first baseman whose glove is neutral and whose speed grades at the 12th percentile, which makes the offensive ceiling the only argument for the lineup spot.

Across 47 innings at AA, Roby posted a 2.1 BB/9 and a 1.0 WHIP, and when that command translates to an MLB context across AAA & AA, the walk rate holds — 2.7 BB/9, comfortably better than the MLB average, with a K-BB% that lands at 15.1%. The strikeout rate is the asterisk: his K/9 translates to 8.5, essentially matching what an average MLB arm produces, which means the profile lives or dies on whether the command stays elite enough to compensate. If it does, he's a useful depth piece who earns a rotation spot in a pinch; if the stuff doesn't miss enough bats against better competition, he settles into a bullpen role where the control still plays.

reports.name: Drew Cavanaugh

Cavanaugh has 35 walks against 55 strikeouts in 227 plate appearances, which translates to an 11.4% walk rate when moved to an MLB context, comfortably above the 8.5% MLB baseline. The MLB-equivalent ISO comes out to .170, just nudging past that same baseline figure of .150, which is fine for a catcher but not the kind of carrying tool that survives a BABIP correction. If the average regresses hard and the power stays modest, you're left with a patient backstop who can work counts at the margin, which is a bench catcher, not a regular.

reports.name: Colton Ledbetter
reports.published_report: The 25 stolen bases are the loudest thing on this card, and they're probably not enough. Ledbetter is hitting .271 at AAA with a .377 BABIP carrying most of it — the translation strips that down to a .137 ISO and a 29% strikeout rate, both of which sit on the wrong side of where you need to be to stick in a corner. The walks (36 in 403 AAA plate appearances) translate to 8.3%, essentially what the average big-leaguer produces, so the discipline isn't the problem, but the power and contact grade are, and both have to improve together for this to be anything more than bench depth. If the strikeouts stay where they are and the BABIP normalizes, what's left is a corner outfielder who can run and not much else.

reports.name: Connor Wietgrefe
reports.published_report: The walk rate is legitimate, the strikeout rate is the problem. Across AAA & AA in 2026, Wietgrefe has posted a 3.0 BB/9 and a 1.20 WHIP over 133.7 innings, and those contact-management numbers translate cleanly enough, but his 7.9 K/9 shrinks to a 7.2 MLB equivalent while the average big-league starter sits at 8.6, and that gap is where the ceiling collapses. A left-hander who misses bats at a below-average clip has to keep the ball on the ground and the walks down every single time out, because there's no swing-and-miss margin to absorb a bad inning. If the command holds at this level, he's a depth arm who eats innings without embarrassing himself; if big-league contact quality exposes the strikeout floor, there's very little left.

report_llm.text: Thirty-four stolen bases across AAA & A+ & A tells you what kind of player this is, and the rest of the profile tells you the ceiling. The walk rate translates to 9.8% at the MLB level, a notch above the 8.5% MLB average, but an MLB-equivalent ISO of .097 sits well short of the .150 MLB average, and speed alone can't close that gap. The hit tool percentiles grade out reasonably, and a .357 OBP across those three levels in 346 plate appearances suggests he can get on base, which is the prerequisite for the speed to matter. If the power doesn't develop, what's left is a fourth outfielder who runs and gets on base at a tick above replacement, which is a bench career, not a regular one.

reports.name: Blake Wolters
reports.published_report: The strikeouts are real enough — 110 across A+ & A translates to a 7.8 K/9 MLB equivalent, but the walks are the whole argument. Fifty-six free passes in 95.3 innings, a 5.3 BB/9 that pairs with a K-BB% sitting at just the 49th percentile while the walk rate checks in at the 38th. The 7.2 ERA is downstream of a profile that doesn't miss enough bats to survive that kind of control, and the 1.6 WHIP says the same thing a different way. If the command cleans up there's a back-end arm in here, but the translated BB/9 comes out at 5.3 against an MLB average of 3.2, and without meaningful improvement on that number, the ceiling the data supports is a depth arm and the floor is the same.

reports.name: Brady Smith
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and the translation is where it gets complicated. Across A+ & A, Brady Smith is punching out hitters at 13.2 per nine over 80.7 innings, 118 strikeouts against 34 walks, and that K-BB% sits in the 94th percentile of the pitcher pool. The problem is that when you run the MLB-equivalent translation, the strikeouts flatten to 8.7 per nine, essentially league average, and the walks translate to 4.2 against a translated K-BB% of 13.1 percent where the MLB average sits at 13.5, meaning the dominant shape at the lower levels becomes a break-even profile one level at a time. The whole case hinges on whether the swing-and-miss travels up the ladder or belongs to the level.

reports.name: Yamal Encarnacion
reports.published_report: The stolen bases carry this profile. Forty-eight at AA across 395 plate appearances is a legitimate weapon, and the 18 K% at that level translates to 21.3% in the majors, right at the 22.0% MLB average, meaning the contact ability that makes the speed playable should survive the climb. The power doesn't travel: a .117 ISO at AA becomes .11 in an MLB context, and the average sits at .15. If the legs and bat-to-ball hold, he's a bench bat who can change a game on the bases; if the speed diminishes even a little, what's left is a second baseman without enough thump to force regular playing time.

reports.published_report:
Two innings. That's the entire current AAA sample, and it's doing almost no work here.

What the translation shows isn't alarming but isn't encouraging: a K/9 that matches the MLB average exactly at 8.6, a BB/9 of 3.8 where the average sits at 3.2, and a K-BB% of 12.4 when the typical MLB starter lands at 13.5. If the strikeout rate doesn't climb and the walks stay where they are, the profile resolves as a depth arm, which is exactly where the ceiling lands anyway. The honest read here is that 2.0 IP can't tell you much, and ValuCast's rankings reflect that uncertainty, sliding him six spots in three days.

reports.name: Wilson Rodriguez
reports.published_report: The walk rate is loud for a 21-year-old at A+: 58 walks across 364 plate appearances, with a translated BB% of 11.4 against a big-league pool that averages 8.5. That's the selling point. The power doesn't come with it — an ISO of .167 at A+ translates to .127 in the majors, meaningfully short of the 8.5 average, and the 20 stolen bases show he knows he has to manufacture something when he does get on. If the plate discipline holds as he climbs and the raw pop develops enough to punish pitchers for nibbling, there's a fringe regular in here; if the power stays where it is, he's a bench piece with a useful OBP, and the ceiling note in the data says the system agrees.
